1	/**
2	 * Zoom limits for the receipt viewer.
3	 *
4	 * 100% means fit-to-viewport, not 1:1 — so a flat maximum percentage means
5	 * different things on different screens. The ceiling is therefore derived from
6	 * the individual image: zoom stops where one image pixel fills one CSS pixel.
7	 * See the "Zoom never invents pixels" invariant in `docs/domain-model.md`.
8	 */
9	
10	export interface FitDimensions {
11		width: number;
12		height: number;
13	}
14	
15	/** The floor, and the meaning of "fit to viewport". */
16	export const MIN_ZOOM = 100;
17	
18	/** Zoom in/out snap to multiples of this. */
19	export const ZOOM_STEP = 50;
20	
21	/**
22	 * The size an image occupies at 100% zoom: scaled down to fit the viewport box,
23	 * never scaled up. An image smaller than the box is already at native size, so
24	 * 100% is also its ceiling.
25	 */
26	export function calculateFitDimensions(
27		naturalWidth: number,
28		naturalHeight: number,
29		viewportWidth: number,
30		viewportHeight: number
31	): FitDimensions {
32		const scale = Math.min(viewportWidth / naturalWidth, viewportHeight / naturalHeight, 1);
33		return { width: naturalWidth * scale, height: naturalHeight * scale };
34	}
35	
36	/**
37	 * The zoom percentage at which the image is displayed at its true resolution —
38	 * the point past which further magnification would only interpolate.
39	 *
40	 * Returns MIN_ZOOM when the image is already at (or below) native size on
41	 * screen, which is what disables the zoom controls: there are no further real
42	 * pixels to show, and a greyed-out control says so honestly.
43	 */
44	export function calculateMaxZoom(naturalWidth: number, baseWidth: number): number {
45		if (baseWidth <= 0) return MIN_ZOOM;
46		return Math.max(MIN_ZOOM, (naturalWidth / baseWidth) * MIN_ZOOM);
47	}

content.text: Reviewed the diff, the three new files, and the pre-change versions for context. Findings, most impactful first. ## 1. `src/lib/utils/imageResize.ts:139` — full-resolution bitmap stays alive across the JPEG encode `bitmap.close()` sits in the `finally` (line 146), so it runs only *after* `await encodeCanvas(canvas, quality)` resolves. The bitmap is dead weight the moment `ctx.drawImage` returns (line 137). For a 12MP HEIC/JPEG that's ~48MB of RGBA held simultaneously with the 2400×1800 canvas backing store (~17MB) and the growing JPEG blob, for the whole duration of the encode — which is the longest step in the function and now runs on files up to the new 25MB `MAX_SOURCE_MB` guard. Cheaper: call `bitmap.close()` on the line right after `ctx.drawImage(...)`, and keep the `finally { bitmap.close(); }` purely as the throw-path safety net — `ImageBitmap.close()` is idempotent (a second call on a detached bitmap is a no-op), so no restructuring is needed. Peak memory during encode drops by the entire source bitmap. Everything else in the resize path is clean: every exit (unsupported type early-return, `getContext` throw, encode reject, success) releases the bitmap, and the second decode via `` + `URL.createObjectURL` is correctly gone. ## 2. `src/lib/services/ReceiptService.ts:244` — the retry closure pins the whole Source File just to read its name `buildReceiptInsert(file, path, extract)` receives the original `File` but uses exactly one thing from it: `sanitizeFilename(file.name)` (line 336).
